Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a massive catch.

Recent findings suggest that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

According to recent reports, europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how swiftly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of fresh car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

According to recent reports, october 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” mentioned Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

Industry observers note that china sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Recent findings suggest that even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

It has been revealed that outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

Recent findings suggest that as the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.
  • It has been revealed that “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, said in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP).
  • Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, said in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.".

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Recent findings suggest that that said, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

It has been revealed that although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

In a recent development, “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some owners might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

Sources indicate that bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That remarked, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

“We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very major signatures,” he said. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

Industry observers note that whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

Sources indicate that andré Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the U.S. Treasury auctioned $15 billion of nine-day cash management bills on Nov. 19, its first sale at that exact term since July 2008. The bills are scheduled to settle Nov. 24 and mature Dec. 3, putting the borrowing across the turn of the month.

Treasury had already flagged a possible short bill in its November financing plan. Its operating cash balance on auction day was within the range it had recorded in 2026. The proceeds were due when the bill settled five days later, so the auction-day balance gives a snapshot of Treasury’s cash before the new borrowing arrived.

Recent findings suggest that the sale reopened a bill first issued on June 4. Investors could buy more of the same security, which kept its Dec. 3 maturity date. Treasury reported a high discount rate of 3.91% and a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.97. The ratio measures the face value of accepted and rejected offers Treasury counted, about $60 billion, against the just over $15 billion it awarded.

Recent findings suggest that treasury auctions cash management bills as needed to meet short-term financing needs. A recent sale ran one day longer. On Oct. 22, Treasury auctioned $25 billion of ten-day bills at a 3.93% high discount rate. Those bills were issued Oct. 26 and matured Nov. 5.

Sources indicate that before the November sale, Treasury’s previous nine-day auction was July 21, 2008, according to its historical auction records. It offered $9 billion at that sale, with a July 22 concern date and July 31 maturity.

Sources indicate that short bills remained in use. The legacy auction series records 29 cash management bill sales with terms of ten days or less after the July 2008 sale, through December 2025. The updated series includes the October and November 2026 auctions.

In its Nov. 4 quarterly refunding statement, Treasury noted it might issue a short-dated bill around the end of November for cash management. It unveiled the offering on Nov. 18 and released the results the next day. The auction documents gave investors the dates for paying Treasury and getting repaid. They identified no specific federal expenses tied to the borrowing.

In a Nov. 20 post on X, @0xCVYH likened the sale to an overdraft, remarked Treasury’s cash had grown tight and argued that the borrowing would help cover end-of-month expenses. The auction schedule confirms that the borrowing spans month-end. The cash data offer a separate check on how unusual Treasury’s balance was at the time.

The Daily Treasury Statement put the Treasury General Account, the government’s operating cash account, at $891.223 billion at the Nov. 19 close, down from $892.310 billion the day before. Across Treasury’s daily balance series through Nov. 19, the 2026 low was $686.969 billion on April 9 and the high was $1.05253 trillion on Oct. 27. Nov. 19 was the latest close available as of Nov. 21. That snapshot gives a sense of scale. Assessing the pressure on Treasury’s cash also requires knowing when receipts and payments are due.

It has been revealed that the nine-day borrowing window starts on Nov. 24, five days after Treasury recorded its auction-day cash balance.

#64459. Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (659 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto 📈 Bullish 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • According to recent reports, we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the tech giant announced aims to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

According to recent reports, we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the tech giant announced aims to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

Recent findings suggest that but don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

Sources indicate that the UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t unveiled any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

Recent findings suggest that I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

It has been revealed that I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost concern - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price slipped to near $61,500 on Friday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a selloff in technology stocks that followed Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut spread to Asian markets and dragged bitcoin to its lowest level since July.
  • Bitcoin first broke below $62,000 on Thursday evening, after Thursday afternoon’s report showed it giving back a rebound toward $64,000.
  • Sources indicate that the selling started in Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price slipped to near $61,500 on Friday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a selloff in technology stocks that followed Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut spread to Asian markets and dragged bitcoin to its lowest level since July.

Bitcoin first broke below $62,000 on Thursday evening, after Thursday afternoon’s report showed it giving back a rebound toward $64,000. The bitcoin price then slid to nearly $61,200 during Asian trading before bouncing back above $61,700. Friday marks a third straight day of losses.

Sources indicate that the selling started in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi slid more than 5%, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down around 6%. The Korea Exchange halted program selling for five minutes after the drop, while Japan’s Nikkei fell as much as 4.85% to a seven-month low.

In a recent development, U.S. futures pointed lower too. Nasdaq-100 futures fell more than 1.7% and S&P 500 futures dropped 0.8%, Yahoo Finance reported. Gold futures lost 3%. The S&P 500 is pointing to a seventh straight daily decline, its longest losing streak since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

It has been revealed that anthropic shares fell 8% in premarket trading after closing their first session at $97.17, up 17% from the $83 IPO price. Nvidia was down about 2.4% and AMD fell nearly 7%, CNBC reported. Hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment, Reuters said.

Bitcoin funds are feeling the pressure. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day outflow since launch. That topped the previous record of $528.3 million set on Jan. 30. The fund bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows earlier this month.

It has been revealed that leveraged traders took heavy losses as the bitcoin price broke support. Bitcoin liquidations hit $712.9 million over 24 hours, with $614 million coming from long positions. Open interest in bitcoin futures fell to $18 billion from $20 billion a week ago, and funding rates flipped broadly negative as traders unwound their bets.

It has been revealed that traders are now watching whether the bitcoin price can hold the $60,000 area. A large pocket of long positions sits in the $60,500 to $60,900 band, just below the current price, and could come into play on a further drop. Bitcoin is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022.

Crypto stocks pointed lower in premarket trading. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $83.90, down about 2.6% from Thursday’s close of $86.13, after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 2.7% to near $106.

Bitcoin miners fell harder. IREN (IREN) dropped about 4.4%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 3.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 3.4%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 3.3%. IREN has also been under pressure as investors reassess AI infrastructure stocks. Delays in bringing some of its capacity online led Microsoft to spend less with the miner than planned last quarter.

Industry observers note that longer-term buyers have not left entirely. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market for bitcoin to date, putting the drawdown at around 54% compared with declines of more than 70% in previous cycles.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,800.

Latest Canadian budget packs funding for 55,000 new EV chargers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 new EV chargers.
  • The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.
  • Sources indicate that “The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 new EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.

Sources indicate that “The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

Recent findings suggest that the rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, upcoming data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

Tech Report: One Bitcoin miner paid an $11.9M tariff bill four years after delivery

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1437 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin miner Bitfarms thought the machines it brought into Washington state in 2021 had been made in Malaysia.
  • It has been revealed that four years later, the company paid the government $11.9 million.
  • Bitfarms disputed the assessment, but its financial statements show it paid in October 2025, after Customs told it the duties were required.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin miner Bitfarms thought the machines it brought into Washington state in 2021 had been made in Malaysia. Its supplier said so, and the company provided US Customs officials with documents supporting that claim.

It has been revealed that four years later, the company paid the government $11.9 million. US Customs and Border Protection had challenged the machines' declared origin, arguing that they were made in China and subject to a 25% import duty.

Bitfarms disputed the assessment, but its financial statements show it paid in October 2025, after Customs told it the duties were required.

Industry observers note that the payment indicates a cost that can follow a mining manufacturer long after its equipment was delivered and started working. Other miners have faced similar disputes over where their machines were made, with one company recently avoiding a potential $100 million assessment and another still contesting an estimate that reached $130 million.

It has been revealed that those numbers don't add up to a single bill for the industry. Each dispute involves different shipments, documents, and decisions, and the outcomes can look very different even when the companies believe they have evidence supporting their declared origins.

Industry observers note that bitfarms' dispute began in early 2022, when Customs challenged the origin of the machines imported the previous year. The manufacturer said its Chinese vendor had represented that the equipment came from Malaysia, while Customs asserted that it was manufactured in China.

The miner submitted supporting documents in the third quarter of 2023 and again in the first quarter of 2025. It also paid $180,000 of the duties in 2024, according to its later filing. As of June 2025, management said it didn't consider a future cash outflow probable and hadn't recorded a provision for the dispute.

Sources indicate that that was an accounting assessment based on what the company knew at the time. In August 2025, Customs responded that duties were required, and Bitfarms reported the payment two months later.

It has been revealed that bitfarms disclosed $180,000 of customs duties paid in 2024 and a separate $11.9 million payment to Customs in October 2025, including interest. The filing’s stated duties and interest components do not reconcile to its reported October payment.

Source: Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements, customs duties note.

Industry observers note that the company hasn't disclosed enough to reconstruct every step of the customs process or establish whether it paid under protest. Nonetheless, its filings do show how a dispute over a shipment can remain relevant to a company's finances long after the initial purchase.

Firm disclosures trace the disputed origin of mining equipment from its arrival in 2021 to a payment in October 2025.

The purchase year did not determine when Bitfarms would pay the customs assessment.

It has been revealed that based on company disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Sources indicate that timeline transcribed from Note 16 of Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements. Dollar figures converted from the stated thousands of US dollars. Milestones are equally spaced for readability, not elapsed time.

It has been revealed that based on tech giant disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Sources indicate that bitfarms has since reorganized under Keel Infrastructure and shifted toward AI and high-performance computing. It paid the customs bill before that transition reached a major milestone: Keel stopped its US Bitcoin mining operations in June 2026 as it prepared sites for other uses.

Other miners have also been shifting power access and data-center sites toward AI, while older import disputes still appear in their financial disclosures.

The money involved can affect how much they have available for equipment and projects, although a disclosed potential charge isn't necessarily money they will have to pay.

Import duties can depend on where a product was made, which sounds simple until a machine contains components from several countries and is assembled elsewhere.

Sources indicate that US customs forms ask importers to identify the product's country of origin. When production takes place in more than one country, the answer can depend on where the product underwent its last substantial transformation, according to Customs' entry instructions.

According to recent reports, the manufacturing process and supporting records can affect the duty owed. The supplier's certificate can support the declared origin, but Customs can still challenge it.

Industry observers note that equipment can also be released and put to work before Customs resolves every issue. Customs uses a process called liquidation to make its final duty calculation for an entry.

Importers can challenge certain decisions through an administrative protest, but deadlines and exceptions depend on the decision being challenged. The public filings don't establish which procedural rules explain every stage of the miners' disputes.

Selling the equipment doesn't automatically settle an importer's customs obligations either. Federal regulations describe duties as a debt owed by the importer, which can be discharged through payment or applicable legal relief.

That doesn't mean the buyer of a secondhand machine automatically inherits the seller's customs bill, since the importer and the terms of any transaction need to be identified separately.

It has been revealed that IREN received a notice in April 2025 concerning hardware it imported between April 2024 and February 2025. Customs asserted that the equipment was of Chinese origin and assessed a 25% tariff, while IREN stated the seller and shipping documents supported a different origin.

It has been revealed that the organization contested an exposure of approximately $100 million. In October 2026, Customs approved its protests and accepted the declared origin of the covered hardware, IREN reported in its September-quarter filing. No additional tariff, administrative fee, or interest is payable for that matter.

Sources indicate that the $100 million was an amount IREN had disputed and no longer has to pay for the covered imports. The company hasn't disclosed enough about the decision to establish whether the same reasoning applies to other shipments or other miners.

Industry observers note that cleanSpark has had a mixed outcome so far. In its June-quarter filing, submitted in August, the miner said Customs had approved some of its protests over machines imported in 2024, while other entries remained contested.

Industry observers note that if Customs prevailed on the remaining entries, CleanSpark estimated that its total tariff liability for the previously purchased machines could reach approximately $130 million, excluding interest. Management considered a loss improbable and recorded no provision as of June 30.

DarkHorse Technologies, previously known as Sphere 3D, faces a smaller claim that indicates how an older equipment purchase can appear in the accounts of a miner with a different name and business plan.

In August, Customs notified DarkHorse that it was asserting Chinese-origin duties on machines purchased in 2022 by a subsidiary acquired in the Cathedra Bitcoin combination.

The tech giant says its subsidiary received certificates from the seller supporting a non-Chinese origin, and it filed a protest in September. Its latest quarterly report puts potential liability at up to $2.3 million, including interest, if Customs prevails. DarkHorse has not recorded a liability.

In a recent development, company estimates if Customs prevails. CleanSpark's was approximately $130 million excluding interest as of June 30. DarkHorse's was up to $2.3 million including interest in its Sept. 30 report. Reporting dates and interest treatment differ.

Source: CleanSpark June 2026 Form 10-Q, Note 15 · DarkHorse September 2026 Form 10-Q, customs duties contingency.

DarkHorse is separately selling its legacy mining fleet as it shifts toward AI infrastructure. Its quarterly report estimated $2.9 million in proceeds, with $1.3 million from machines sold by Sept. 30.

In a recent development, bitfarms reported a payment, IREN's covered assessment has been resolved, CleanSpark's estimate excludes interest, and DarkHorse's includes it. Adding them together would treat a past payment and an avoided charge as outstanding bills.

CleanSpark's remaining protests and DarkHorse's challenge will determine whether either miner faces a further payment on the disputed imports.

IREN's result reveals that a challenge can succeed, while Bitfarms' earlier payment shows why investors can't assume that a organization's initial accounting assessment will be the final word.

#64452. Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1247 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

It has been revealed that according to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

It has been revealed that this isn’t new in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

According to recent reports, A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Sources indicate that now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

According to recent reports, waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

It has been revealed that since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

Industry observers note that in other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

In a recent development, the penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

Industry observers note that and Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

People have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

It has been revealed that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

Recent findings suggest that NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.
  • In a recent development, the price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000.
  • Industry observers note that the margin is thin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.

In a recent development, the price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000. The realized price is a measure of what holders paid, not where the market trades. When bitcoin trades above it, the typical coin is sitting on a gain. Below it, the typical coin is underwater.

Industry observers note that the margin is thin. The firm noted the MVRV ratio, which compares bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, sits “just above 1.” A reading of 1 means the market price has fallen all the way to the realized price.

Sources indicate that realized price values each coin at the price it last moved on the blockchain, then averages across the supply. Look Into Bitcoin describes it as bitcoin’s average cost basis. Because it tracks the price when coins last changed hands, it moves far more slowly than the market.

The MVRV ratio expresses the same idea as a multiple. Above 1, holders are in profit on average. Below 1, they are not. A reading just above 1 means the market price is only a sliver higher than what the average coin cost.

Sources indicate that the firm did not give the exact realized price in its post, which included a chart. That leaves the exact cushion between today’s price and the average cost basis unstated. Bitcoin Magazine Pro’s full realized price chart sits behind a login, so the current level could not be confirmed independently for this report.

“The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit,” the firm wrote. “The margin is thin.”.

It has been revealed that the slide has come with heavy selling from funds. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost about $541 million on Thursday, its largest one-day outflow since it launched in January 2024, Bloomberg reported. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total that day.

It has been revealed that the selling stands out against the buying earlier in the fall. Institutions piled into bitcoin ETFs through the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record, Bitcoin Magazine reported this week.

Industry observers note that leveraged traders took losses too. More than $700 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and about 86% of them were bets on higher prices. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $200 million of the total.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop is part of a longer downturn rather than the start of a new one. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he said in a note dated Nov. 18.

The note frames Friday’s price action as a late stage of a decline that began well before November. Butterfill pointed to whale selling that weighed on prices from late 2025, expectations of higher interest rates and weakness in technology stocks, all of which have kept buyers cautious.

Industry observers note that “Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said. “Geopolitics will have a considerable say in that.”.

A move through the realized price would put bitcoin near the bottom edge of that range. The firm said holders as a group have not been in loss since early 2023.

A sustained breakout, Butterfill stated, would likely require “a change in the policy outlook, renewed whale participation or both.”.

A few hours later, ArbitrageX’s lending tracker estimated that $239.8 million in collateral across its sample could become eligible for liquidation in a reference-price range of about $52,700 to $54,300. The positions included several tokenized versions of Bitcoin.

On Aave, a position becomes eligible for liquidation when its health factor falls below one. The new N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

In a recent development, the all-electric Denza N8 starts at 269,900 yuan, or about $40,500, with prices ranging up to 329,900 yuan ($49,500) for the Flagship model. The PHEV models start at 300,900 yuan and 32,900 yuan, respectively.

BYD added a few premium extras like front and rear zero-gravity seats, a drop-down ceiling entertainment screen, ambient lighting, and wireless phone chargers.

According to recent reports, the Denza N8 is offered with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD variant uses a single motor that delivers either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp), depending on the configuration.

In a recent development, the tri-motor Denza N8 debuts BYD’s e3 Evo technology. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

BYD’s Denza said the N8 EV boasts an all-electric CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles), “making it the world’s longest-range mass-produced all-electric SUV.”.

To put it in perspective, that’s as much as the outgoing N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

It’s available with two second-gen BYD Blade battery packs: 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of up to 885 km (549 miles) and 1,003 km (623 miles).

According to recent reports, with BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its fresh luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

BYD also sells the extended Denza N8L in China, which went on sale earlier this year, starting at 299,800 yuan ($45,000).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block noted in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.
  • In a recent development, the report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S.
  • Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block noted in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

In a recent development, the report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

It has been revealed that coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Industry observers note that small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

Customers also came back. Among Cash App people who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

In a recent development, the activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

Square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

Industry observers note that block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the firm said.

Sources indicate that A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

According to recent reports, block noted Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block mentioned.

Singapore’s central bank plans to help develop a common way for banks to verify who an AI agent represents and what the customer has authorized it to do. Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), outlined the proposal on Nov. 19 at the Singapore FinTech Festival. A separate Singapore sandbox would test safeguards for AI agent payments, with stablecoins and tokenized deposits among the options.

Under the proposed know-your-agent protocol, a financial institution would receive information about the agent’s identity, the customer it acts for, its delegated authority and the rules it must follow. The protocol would also convey any assurances about the agent’s origin and reliability. The institution could use that information to set the scope of access and give the agent a dedicated, secure channel.

Chia said the customer’s mandate should specify the actions the agent may take and the limits and conditions on them. The more discretion the agent has or the greater the potential impact, the stronger the controls should be. MAS intends to help develop the protocol in the next phase of its Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime initiative.

MAS and the Future of Finance Institute declared the planned Agentic Money Sandbox on Nov. 18. The institute would set up a controlled environment for institutions to test payments and corporate treasury management with digital money ahead of any live deployment.

Singapore has proposed a way to check an agent’s authority and separate sandbox trials for payments and corporate treasury.

The proposed payment trial would put the identity and authority checks at the bank or payment provider before execution.

The proposed treasury trial separates the company’s mandate from the bank’s terms for accepting an instruction.

The customer sets the mandate. The bank or payment provider sets controls before acting on an instruction.

MAS aims to help develop the protocol. The diagrams show the proposed trials and examples of digital money.

According to recent reports, the arrows show who would pass an instruction to whom under the approach Chia Der Jiun outlined at the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov. 19. The selectable views compare the two proposed trials.

Recent findings suggest that MAS aims to help develop the protocol. The diagrams show the proposed trials and examples of digital money.

According to recent reports, in the proposed payments test, the participating bank or payment provider would verify the agent’s identity and authority and apply risk controls before executing an instruction. Chia cited tokenized deposits and stablecoins as examples of the digital money the trial could use.

Recent findings suggest that in the treasury test, a company would define what its agent could do. The agent could monitor cash balances and upcoming payments, decide when and where funds should move, and use tokenized deposits for permitted transfers. The bank would set its own controls and terms for accepting each instruction.

Sources indicate that in a Nov. 18 speech, Singapore Deputy Prime Minister and MAS Chairman Gan Kim Yong gave the example of an agent making a payment under a contract once the relevant terms had been met and checked. The joint release named DBS, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB as the institute’s launch partners. The same release gave no sandbox start date or participant list.

Gan stated institutions and companies remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf. Chia asked who bears responsibility when an agent makes a mistake or exceeds its mandate.

Lenders had about 1.14 billion USDC available to withdraw late on Nov. 20. If borrowing hits the latest cap and deposits stay at 4.19 billion USDC, about 190 million USDC would remain for withdrawals.

Aave's Ethereum Core market had 4.19 billion USDC supplied and 3.05 billion borrowed at 22:11 UTC on Nov. 20, according to an Aave API snapshot published by Aave Tracker. According to recent reports, the address, 0x176F…a132, supplied 400 million USDC and 350 million USDC in two transactions about eight minutes apart on Nov. 19. The same wallet received Aave's receipt tokens from both deposits.

Four minutes and 24 seconds after the change, the same wallet supplied another 738 million USDC, bringing its deposits to 1,488 million USDC over about 75 minutes.

Sources indicate that coindaro reported that at 17:43 UTC on Nov. 19 the wallet held about 1.495 billion in aEthUSDC, the token that represents its deposits and accrued interest. At that same reading, the market had 4.228 billion USDC supplied and 2.604 billion borrowed, leaving roughly 1.62 billion unborrowed. At Ethereum block 26,459,205, just before 22:11 UTC on Nov. 20, on-chain balances showed the address holding about 1.495 billion aEthUSDC, or 35.7% of the receipt token's supply.

LlamaRisk recommended the higher borrowing limit on Nov. 20 after loans reached 98.5% of the previous $2.7 billion cap. Aave put the change into effect at 11:15 UTC. The amount of cash in the pool changes when people actually borrow, deposit, repay or withdraw.

Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S.
  • Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m.
  • In a recent development, the break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower.

Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data. The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000.

In a recent development, the break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss.

Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower.

Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry.

Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed. Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield.

Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.

JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June.BTC is now less than 4% away from a new cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz.

Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

According to recent reports, leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.

In a recent development, the move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

In a recent development, crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session. Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.

Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

According to recent reports, data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.

The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

Russia allows Bitcoin trading as sanctioned Moscow Exchange prepares December launch

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 22, Russian exchanges can begin trading Bitcoin once the central bank approves the rules, but customers still can't use it to pay for anything.
  • It has been revealed that moscow Exchange aims a Dec.
  • The central bank's retail purchase rules took effect Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from Nov. 22, Russian exchanges can begin trading Bitcoin once the central bank approves the rules, but customers still can't use it to pay for anything.

It has been revealed that moscow Exchange aims a Dec. 1 pilot through a US-sanctioned clearinghouse, with ordinary investors limited to 300,000 rubles in annual purchases per intermediary.

The central bank's retail purchase rules took effect Nov. 17, limiting ordinary investors to Bitcoin, Ethereum and the dollar-linked stablecoin USDT. A separate ordinance governing exchange operations allows venues to begin trading from Nov. 22, provided the regulator has approved their trading rules.

Moscow Exchange aims to launch on Dec. 1, starting with pilot transactions as participating firms connect. The newly introduced market will let investors buy crypto through familiar financial intermediaries while prohibiting its use in everyday domestic payments.

The allowance covers purchases through a single intermediary during a calendar year.

If you buy 100,000 rubles' worth of Bitcoin and another 100,000 rubles' worth of Ethereum (about $1,200) through the same broker, you've used two-thirds of the allowance, regardless of what the coins are worth a week later.

It has been revealed that purchases can also go through asset managers and registered crypto exchange offices, including deals arranged outside an exchange's order book. The limit is measured in rubles spent on purchases, rather than the market value of the investor's holdings.

Qualified investors can buy other coins without the same purchase cap, although they must pass a test and review the risks before trading, just as ordinary investors do.

The central bank chose Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the retail list partly because they're heavily traded and have at least five years of price history on foreign exchanges.

Exchanges must register the companies trading there, track orders and completed transactions, calculate market prices, and report activity to the central bank.

Recent findings suggest that russia's new crypto law also provides for digital depositories that record asset ownership rights. They are part of the exchange and custody framework the new market will need once trading begins.

Recent findings suggest that owning Bitcoin through that system still won't let someone spend it at a Russian shop. Domestic merchants remain barred from accepting cryptocurrency for goods and services.

Exporters and importers can use it under a separate provision for cross-border settlement. A broker can help a customer exchange rubles for Bitcoin, and an exporter can receive Bitcoin for a shipment abroad, but a restaurant in Moscow still has to charge for lunch in something else.

Moscow Exchange already has a market for investors who want exposure to Bitcoin's price. By mid-September, it reported more than 600 billion rubles in crypto-futures turnover since its first contracts began trading in the summer of 2025.

Those cash-settled contracts pay gains or losses in rubles as crypto prices move, without delivering the underlying assets. The December pilot would trade the assets themselves, so the futures figure tells us little about how much Bitcoin investors will want to buy and hold through the latest system.

The exchange's technical specification describes same-day and next-day settlement, while the National Clearing Centre's published market plan lists five trading pairs: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT against rubles, plus Bitcoin and USDT against USDX, a specialized settlement currency used by the clearinghouse.

The exchange isn't planning direct BTC/USDT trading for the initial launch, although it may consider crypto-to-crypto pairs in 2027.

Members will be able to place anonymous orders or negotiate deals with known counterparties, and the clearinghouse expects to process settlements roughly every 30 to 60 minutes.

Short selling will initially be prohibited on the exchange, although brokers may offer margin trading under the applicable rules.

One large deal arranged in advance could lift the day's turnover without creating the steady stream of buyers and sellers that an ordinary investor needs.

In a recent development, the clearinghouse's FAQ also explains how the cryptocurrency will move once a trade is completed. Settlement will take place through accounts maintained at a separate digital depository outside the Moscow Exchange group, without a corresponding blockchain transaction for every trade.

When one participant buys Bitcoin from another, the depository can upgrade its records of who holds the rights to those assets while the underlying coins stay in custody. That allows the exchange to process trades without sending Bitcoin between public wallets every time an order is matched.

The arrangement makes the depository's identity and the rules for moving assets into and out of its custody particularly important. Moscow Exchange has described the proposed account structure, but the published materials reviewed don't identify a separate depository or confirm whether customers can withdraw their holdings directly to personal wallets.

The market is initially intended for existing qualified trading and clearing participants, with brokers responsible for determining which customers can use their services.

Moscow Exchange notes it will use the National Clearing Centre to clear the trades, relying on infrastructure already familiar to its stock-market participants.

The US Treasury sanctioned both Moscow Exchange and the National Clearing Centre in June 2024. That adds a complication for the planned USDT market, which the exchange intends to introduce initially through a pilot with restricted trading volumes.

The technical specification identifies USDT as issued on Ethereum, meaning a company outside Russia controls the underlying token. Tether has a policy for freezing wallets associated with people or entities on US sanctions lists, although that policy alone doesn't establish what will happen to any particular wallet used by Moscow Exchange or its clearing and custody partners.

Settling individual trades through depository accounts reduces the need to move tokens on a public blockchain, but the underlying USDT still has to be held somewhere.

The exchange hasn't identified the wallets that will hold those tokens, explained who will supply them, or described how Tether's sanctions controls would apply to the custody arrangement.

No freeze connected to the proposed pilot has been verified, and the available documents don't establish whether Tether has reviewed the arrangement.

The first trades in December may be deals clients already make elsewhere, brought onto Moscow Exchange's books.

If the pilot proceeds, repeat trading and the ability to buy or sell near the quoted price will tell us whether a usable market is taking shape.

For USDT, the exchange and its partners will also have to show they can hold the underlying tokens and complete settlement through the proposed depository, with the issuer's sanctions policy still unresolved.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a bigger Federal Reserve rate hike, even as bitcoin broke below $60,000 for the first time since July and stocks sank on bets that the Fed will keep tightening into a selloff.
  • Industry observers note that bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec.
  • He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a bigger Federal Reserve rate hike, even as bitcoin broke below $60,000 for the first time since July and stocks sank on bets that the Fed will keep tightening into a selloff.

Industry observers note that bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. He cited the energy supply shock and a drop in crude prices as reasons for the central bank to hold back.

He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year. Bessent noted it “seems somewhat peripatetic” to want the bigger increase only 11 or 12 months later. He did not name the governor.

“I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards,” Bessent mentioned.

The comments came two days after Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC a half-point hike is probably necessary in December and that the central bank may need to “shock people.” Waller noted inflation is “headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”.

Recent findings suggest that waller is not alone. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike in December, and two floated a larger one. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also declined to rule out a bigger move on Thursday.

It has been revealed that “We’ve now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters. “So everything’s always on the table.”.

Not everyone wants to go bigger. New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.” St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027.

The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years and held them steady in October. Inflation has stayed hot since the Iran strikes pushed up energy prices earlier this year.

Citi still expects a quarter-point increase in December. Global chief economist Nathan Sheets said Thursday he does not see a need for 50 basis points despite persistent inflation. In a note Friday, the bank wrote that “Fed officials will consequently have little appetite to hike into an equity sell-off.”.

Citi expects the Fed to hold after December and begin cutting later in 2027. Traders agree on the next step: the CME Group’s FedWatch tool highlighted a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point hike, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 10 basis points to 4.95% as investors bought bonds.

Stocks fell for another day. The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 2% in morning trading, and the VIX volatility index topped 30, its highest level since March.

Bitcoin traded near $59,700 shortly before 11 a.m. ET, down more than 5% on the day, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. It broke below $60,000 for the first time since early July and is on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2022.

Higher rates are a headwind for assets that pay no yield, and the selloff has reached companies that hold bitcoin. Strategy’s stock fell for a sixth straight session on Thursday, and the bitcoin price has dropped roughly 25% in a month, a slide Bitcoin Magazine tracked earlier this week.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill tied the outlook to inflation in a note dated Nov. 18. “Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,300.
